newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybean prices drop, palladium soars.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybean prices drop, palladium soars.

text.p: Corn and soybean prices fell on Tuesday as weather forecasts for a cool week and a wet weekend in the Midwest doused worries about crop stress and triggered selling by speculators.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November closed 11-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $6.34-1/2. December corn fell 7-3/4 cents a bushel to close at $2.57-1/4.
Forecaster Weather Services Corp said a storm system in the Midwest was expected to produce 0.25 to 1.00 inch of rain this weekend with 40 to 60 percent coverage in the Corn Belt.
Some long-range outlooks suggested a shift to a wetter pattern, a scenario that would aid developing soybean crops.

The National Weather Service 6-to-10-day outlook released on Monday called for below normal temperatures and above normal precipitation across much of the Midwest. That forecast covers the period from August 10 to 14.
"There is rain in the forecast and there's no heat," said trader Vic Lespinasse at Dean Witter. "That's a very bearish combination."
In New York, palladium continued to soar on worries about future supplies from Russia and South Africa.
Both platinum and palladium are used in manufacturing of automobiles and electronics.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, palladium for September delivery rose the $12.00 an ounce daily limit to close at $227.60, a new life-of contract high for the third straight day.
Palladium was quoted at a new 17-year high at $245.50 in London earlier on Tuesday.
Short supplies are driving the rally.

No further Russian shipments of platinum group metals are expected in Japan under an annual supply contract until around August 10, and offerings by Russia in the spot market are not meeting pent-up demand, traders said.
"The underlying rate of demand growth for palladium is running at double digit figures," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said in a report.
"Up until recently it was generally assumed by most observers, including ourselves, that the Russians would go on meeting this demand increase from mine production and stockpile material," he said.

"Now we are beginning to have serious doubts about this assumption," he said. ""They must realize that the West's car and electronics industries could live with $250 to $300 an ounce palladium for a few years before major substitution or thrifting was seen."

A strike overnight at South Africa's Impala Platinum Ltd was also adding to supply concerns, even though management said production was expected to run close to normal levels "in the short to medium term".
South Africa and Russia are the world's main suppliers of platinum and palladium.
Platinum prices swung wildly during the day, reflecting the uncertainty about supplies.
October platinum ended down $5.60 an ounce at $449.60 but not before setting a new life-of-contract high early at $466.00, then swinging through a wide $26.50 range.
Oil prices ended mixed as many traders squared positions ahead of weekly U.S. oil inventory from the American Petroleum Institute to be released on Tuesday evening.
September gasoline closed up 0.36 cent at 67.10 cents a gallon. Weekly gasoline stocks were expected to have fallen about two million barrels due to continued high demand.
September crude ended six cents a barrel higher at $20.81, shrugging off news Iraq was taking its final procedural step for restarting oil sales under a United Nations plan.

"There was some expected positioning before the APIs, but part of it too is that the market will not respond to Iraqi oil sales until the exports themselves actually start to become feature of overall supply," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.

Iraq submitted its oil pricing formula to the U.N. in the final step to resume its second six months of oil sales. If there is no hitch in approving the formula, it is expected that Iraq could restart oil exports as early as this weekend.
Under the terms of the "oil-for-food" deals between Iraq and the U.N., Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal installments.
September heating oil ended down 0.12 cent at 58.32 cents.
